claim: CaNAR2 was engineered as an improved version of CaNAR1 by optimizing the donor and acceptor fluorescent protein pair.
source: To investigate the spatiotemporal regulation of calcineurin signaling in response to Ca2+ oscillations in β-cells, we engineered an improved version of our previously described FRET-based calcineurin activity reporter (CaNAR) (Newman and Zhang, 2008) by optimizing the donor and acceptor fluorescent protein pair (Figure 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states the engineering of CaNAR2 and references Figure 1 which shows the optimization process.

claim: CaNAR2 exhibits at least twofold greater response compared to CaNAR1 when treated with thapsigargin or ionomycin.
source: (B and C) Representative time-courses comparing the yellow/cyan (Y/C) emission ratio changes from CaNAR1 and CaNAR2 in HEK293 cells treated with (B) 1 μM thapsigargin (TG) or (C) 1 μM ionomycin (iono). CaNAR2 exhibits an at least twofold greater response in each condition.
evidence: Direct comparison data shown in Figure 1B and 1C demonstrating the improved response of CaNAR2.

claim: Ca2+ oscillations induce distinct temporal patterns of calcineurin activity in the cytosol and plasma membrane versus at the ER and mitochondria in MIN6 β-cells.
source: We show that Ca2+ oscillations induce distinct temporal patterns of calcineurin activity in the cytosol and plasma membrane vs at the ER and mitochondria in these cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Differential calcineurin activity patterns are determined by variations in the subcellular distribution of calmodulin (CaM).
source: Furthermore, we found that these differential calcineurin activity patterns are determined by variations in the subcellular distribution of calmodulin (CaM), indicating that CaM plays an active role in shaping both the spatial and temporal aspects of calcineurin signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental manipulations of CaM levels.

claim: Membrane depolarization induced by tetraethylammonium chloride (TEA) treatment produces robust oscillations in RCaMP fluorescence intensity in MIN6 cells.
source: Membrane depolarization induced by tetraethylammonium chloride (TEA) treatment produced robust oscillations in RCaMP fluorescence intensity, which were consistent with the cytosolic Ca2+ oscillations previously observed in MIN6 cells (Landa et al., 2005; Ni et al., 2010) (Figure 2F–I, red curves).
evidence: Direct observation of Ca2+ oscillations using RCaMP reporter, with citation to previous studies showing similar patterns.

claim: Cytosolic and plasma membrane-targeted CaNAR2 exhibit integrating, step-like patterns of calcineurin activity in response to TEA-induced Ca2+ oscillations.
source: Using both cytosolic and plasma membrane-targeted CaNAR2, we were able to observe integrating, step-like patterns of calcineurin activity in response to TEA-induced Ca2+ oscillations, with each step-increase in calcineurin activity synchronized to a cytosolic Ca2+ peak, as measured by RCaMP (Figure 2F,G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Direct observation using targeted biosensors shown in Figure 2F and 2G.

claim: Mitochondrial and ER-targeted CaNAR2 exhibit reversible, oscillatory responses to cytosolic Ca2+ oscillations.
source: To our surprise, however, mitochondrial and ER-targeted CaNAR2 both exhibited far more reversible responses to cytosolic Ca2+ oscillations (Figure 2H,I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Direct observation using targeted biosensors shown in Figure 2H and 2I.

claim: ER-targeted CaNAR2 exhibits almost perfect calcineurin activity oscillations upon TEA stimulation.
source: This difference was particularly striking for erCaNAR2, which exhibited almost perfect calcineurin activity oscillations upon TEA stimulation.
evidence: Direct observation from experimental data with erCaNAR2.

claim: The differential response patterns of CaNAR2 are independent of biosensor expression level.
source: Furthermore, these response patterns were independent of the CaNAR expression level (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that they reflect genuine differences in endogenous calcineurin signaling.
evidence: Control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 testing different expression levels.

claim: PKA phosphorylates multiple residues in NFAT.
source: Notably, PKA phosphorylates multiple residues in NFAT (Beals et al., 1997; Sheridan et al., 2002), and PKA has repeatedly been shown to antagonize calcineurin signaling in the regulation of a variety of cellular processes such as exocytosis (Lester et al., 2001), excitation-contraction coupling (Santana et al., 2002), and mitochondrial division (Cribbs and Strack, 2007).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Blocking PKA activity with H89 abolishes erCaNAR2 oscillations and leads to a delayed but pronounced increase in the CaNAR response.
source: Blocking PKA activity by treating TEA-stimulated MIN6 cells with the PKA inhibitor H89 appeared to abolish erCaNAR2 oscillations, leading to a delayed but pronounced increase in the CaNAR response (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: H89 treatment completely abolishes Ca2+ oscillations in TEA-stimulated MIN6 cells.
source: In addition, H89 treatment completely abolished the Ca2+ oscillations, which is consistent with the behavior of a previously described Ca2+/cAMP/PKA oscillatory circuit in MIN6 β-cells (Ni et al., 2010).
evidence: Experimental observation with citation to previous work describing the oscillatory circuit.

claim: The increased erCaNAR2 response following H89 treatment is specifically caused by calcineurin activity.
source: Despite the apparent lack of Ca2+ signaling, the observed increase in the erCaNAR2 response was nonetheless specifically caused by calcineurin activity, as the increase could be blocked by addition of the calcineurin inhibitor cyclosporin A prior to H89 treatment (Figure 3E).
evidence: Control experiment using calcineurin inhibitor shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Addition of PKC inhibitor Gö6983 to TEA-stimulated MIN6 cells results in a steadily increasing erCaNAR2 response accompanied by a transition from Ca2+ oscillations to persistently elevated cytosolic Ca2+ levels.
source: Moreover, addition of the PKC inhibitor Gö6983 to TEA-stimulated MIN6 cells also resulted in a steadily increasing erCaNAR2 response, accompanied by a transition from Ca2+ oscillations to persistently elevated cytosolic Ca2+ levels (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: TEA functions by blocking plasma membrane K+ channels, leading to membrane depolarization and activation of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
source: TEA functions by blocking plasma membrane K+ channels, leading to membrane depolarization, and thereby activating voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Hille, 1967; Wang and Greer, 1995).
evidence: Statement of established mechanism with citations to previous work.

claim: Direct addition of KCl promotes depolarization-induced Ca2+ influx in electrically excitable cells such as β-cells.
source: The direct addition of KCl also promotes depolarization-induced Ca2+ influx in electrically excitable cells such as β-cells (Bianchi and Shanes, 1959; Powell et al., 1984; Bading et al., 1993; Graef et al., 1999; Macías et al., 2001; Everett and Cooper, 2013), and repeated cycles of KCl addition and wash-out were successfully able to mimic TEA-stimulated oscillations in cytosolic Ca2+ levels and ER-localized calcineurin activity in MIN6 cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations and experimental demonstration in Figure 4A.

claim: H89 treatment results in an integrative, step-like response from erCaNAR2 during repeated KCl-induced Ca2+ spikes.
source: Using this approach, we found that the addition of H89 resulted in an integrative, step-like response from erCaNAR2 (Figure 4B), much like that seen with cytoCaNAR2 in TEA-stimulated cells (Figure 2F), although RCaMP did not appear to respond under these conditions.
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ca2+ spikes can be detected using the higher affinity probe YC-Nano50 even when RCaMP does not respond in the presence of H89.
source: However, we were able to confirm the generation of Ca2+ spikes using a higher affinity probe, YC-Nano50 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Horikawa et al., 2010).
evidence: Control experiment using alternative Ca2+ sensor shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: PKC inhibitor Gö6983 does not alter the oscillatory response of erCaNAR2 to successive KCl treatments.
source: In contrast to H89 treatment, the inclusion of Gö6983 to inhibit PKC activity did not appear to alter the response of erCaNAR2 to successive KCl treatments (Figure 4C).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PKA activity, but not PKC activity, antagonizes calcineurin near the ER surface in MIN6 cells.
source: Our findings indicated that PKA activity, but not PKC activity, antagonizes calcineurin near the ER surface, thereby giving rise to ER-localized calcineurin activity oscillations in MIN6 cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the differential effects of H89 and Gö6983 on erCaNAR2 responses.

claim: TEA-stimulated PKA activity reaches 55.4 ± 5.9% of maximum in the cytosol and 39.8 ± 3.3% at the ER (p = 0.0249).
source: Interestingly, we detected slightly less PKA activity at the ER, with TEA-stimulated AKAR4 responses reaching 55.4 ± 5.9% and 39.8 ± 3.3% (p = 0.0249) of the maximum dynamic range in the cytosol and at the ER, respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: Quantitative measurement using AKAR4 biosensors shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Setting PKA activity to maximum levels using IBMX pretreatment does not affect the subcellular CaNAR response patterns.
source: We also found that setting PKA activity to maximum levels using IBMX pretreatment in conjunction with KCl stimulation, thus clamping PKA activity in these regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), did not affect the subcellular CaNAR response patterns (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: Control experiment shown in Figure 5E-H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Calcineurin exists as a stable heterodimer between a regulatory subunit (CNB) and a catalytic subunit (CNA).
source: Calcineurin exists as a stable heterodimer between a regulatory subunit (CNB) and a catalytic subunit (CNA) and becomes activated when Ca2+-bound CaM (Ca2+/CaM) binds to the regulatory arm of CNA, thus driving a conformational change that removes calcineurin from its basal, auto-inhibited state (Rusnak and Mertz, 2000; Wang et al., 2008; Rumi-Masante et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement of established mechanism with citations to previous work.

claim: CaNARi exhibits a robust increase in the cyan-to-yellow fluorescence emission ratio in response to cytosolic Ca2+ elevation in HEK293 cells.
source: The resulting Calcineurin Activation Ratiometric indicator, or CaNARi, exhibited a robust increase in the cyan-to-yellow fluorescence emission ratio, which tracked closely with the increase in Ca2+ detected using RCaMP, in response to cytosolic Ca2+ elevation in HEK293 cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The CaNARi response is dependent on the binding of Ca2+/CaM, as it can be blocked by pretreatment with the CaM antagonist W7.
source: This Ca2+-induced FRET change could be blocked by pretreatment with the membrane-permeable CaM antagonist W7, indicating that the CaNARi response is in fact dependent on the binding of Ca2+/CaM (Figure 6C).
evidence: Control experiment using CaM antagonist shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The responses from targeted CaNARi variants are similar in all examined subcellular compartments.
source: However, in contrast to the subcellular CaNAR responses, the responses from the targeted CaNARi variants were similar in all of the subcellular compartments that we examined (Figure 7C–F).
evidence: Direct comparison of CaNARi responses across different subcellular locations shown in Figure 7C-F.

claim: The kinetics of calcineurin activation are similar throughout the cell under Ca2+ oscillation conditions.
source: These results indicate that the kinetics of calcineurin activation are similar throughout the cell under these conditions.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the uniform CaNARi responses across subcellular compartments.

claim: Mitochondrial and ER-targeted CaNARi exhibit slightly smaller TEA-stimulated responses compared with cytosolic and plasma membrane probes.
source: In fact, a closer inspection of the subcellularly targeted CaNARi responses revealed that both mitochondrial and ER-targeted CaNARi exhibited slightly smaller TEA-stimulated responses compared with the cytosolic and plasma membrane probes (Figure 7B).
evidence: Quantitative comparison shown in Figure 7B.

claim: There is no correlation between CaNARi response amplitude and biosensor expression level.
source: We also observed no correlation between the CaNARi response amplitude and the biosensor expression level (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting this difference was not an artifact of reporter expression.
evidence: Control analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: A slightly lower amount of Ca2+ is detected near the ER surface compared to the cytosol (71.4% vs 61.2% of max Ca2+, p = 0.0049).
source: In addition, only a small difference was observed when we compared the magnitude of these local Ca2+ signals, with a slightly lower amount of Ca2+ near the ER surface than in the cytosol (71.4% of max Ca2+ in the cytosol vs 61.2% at the ER, p = 0.0049).
evidence: Quantitative measurement using GCaMP3 sensors.

claim: The concentration of free CaM often reaches only 75 nM.
source: Indeed, the concentration of free CaM often reaches only 75 nM (Persechini and Stemmer, 2002; Wu and Bers, 2007; Saucerman and Bers, 2012), whereas CaM targets can be in excess of 20 μM (Saucerman and Bers, 2012).
evidence: Statement of established values with citations to previous work.

claim: Ca2+/CaM would only diffuse approximately 0.1 μm before Ca2+ begins to dissociate.
source: Similarly, based on the kinetics of Ca2+ binding to and dissociation from the N- and C-lobes of CaM, it was calculated that Ca2+/CaM would only diffuse ∼0.1 μm before Ca2+ begins to dissociate, suggesting that Ca2+/CaM primarily acts as a highly localized signal (Saucerman and Bers, 2012).
evidence: Statement based on calculations from previous work with citation.

claim: A significantly lower FRET response is observed when BSCaM-2 is tethered to the ER surface compared to when it diffuses freely through the cytosol (p < 0.0001).
source: Our model predicts that free Ca2+/CaM is less abundant in the vicinity of the ER compared with the bulk cytosol (Figure 9A, left), and indeed we observed a significantly lower (p < 0.0001) FRET response when BSCaM-2 was tethered to the ER surface than when it was able to diffuse freely through the cytosol (Figure 9B), suggesting that less Ca2+/CaM is present near the ER.
evidence: Quantitative measurement using BSCaM-2 biosensor shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Overexpressing mCherry-tagged CaM rescues most of the difference between the ER and cytosolic FRET responses of BSCaM-2.
source: More importantly, we found that overexpressing mCherry-tagged CaM was able to rescue most of the difference between the ER and cytosolic FRET responses (Figure 9B, 'ER+CaM').
evidence: Experimental manipulation shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Co-expression of CaM-mCherry alongside erCaNAR2 results in integrated calcineurin activity responses similar to those seen in the cytosol.
source: Remarkably, combining mCherry-tagged CaM overexpression with the application of repeated, KCl-induced Ca2+ transients in CaNAR-expressing cells reveals that this is indeed the case. In contrast to cells expressing erCaNAR2 alone, which exhibit oscillatory FRET responses in response to repeated KCl stimulation and washout (Figure 9C), the co-expression of CaM-mCherry alongside erCaNAR2 clearly results in integrated calcineurin activity responses similar to those seen in the cytosol (Figure 9D).
evidence: Direct experimental comparison shown in Figure 9C and 9D.

claim: Pretreating cells with 20 μM W7 gives rise to oscillatory responses from cytoCaNAR2.
source: Conversely, reducing the amount of available Ca2+/CaM should lead to ER-like CaNAR oscillations in the cytosol. Indeed, pretreating cells with a low dose (20 μM) of the CaM antagonist W7 gave rise to oscillatory responses from cytoCaNAR2, in contrast to integrating responses in cells lacking W7 pretreatment (Figure 9E,F).
evidence: Direct experimental comparison shown in Figure 9E and 9F.

claim: Free concentrations of Ca2+/CaM are limiting near the ER surface and significantly modulate local Ca2+ oscillation-induced calcineurin activity dynamics.
source: Taken together, our results strongly suggest that free concentrations of Ca2+/CaM are limiting near the ER surface and thus significantly modulate the local, Ca2+ oscillation-induced calcineurin activity dynamics in this subcellular region.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental manipulations of CaM levels.

claim: Calcineurin responses in cortical neurons treated with amyloid-β peptide differ subcellularly, with more rapid activation in dendritic spines than in the cytosol and nucleus.
source: Recently, calcineurin responses in cortical neurons treated with the amyloid-β peptide were shown to differ subcellularly, with more rapid calcineurin activation occurring in dendritic spines than in the cytosol and nucleus (Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement of previous findings with citation.

claim: Calcineurin dynamics are predicted to differ significantly within the dyadic cleft and cytosol in cardiomyocytes.
source: Calcineurin dynamics are also predicted to differ significantly within the dyadic cleft and cytosol in cardiomyocytes (Saucerman and Bers, 2008).
evidence: Statement of previous predictions with citation.

claim: Ca2+ oscillations are responsible for driving the pulsatile secretion of insulin in pancreatic β-cells.
source: Ca2+ oscillations are responsible for driving the pulsatile secretion of insulin (Hellman et al., 1992; Tengholm and Gylfe, 2008), and the chronic inhibition of calcineurin, which is a common form of immunosuppressive therapy, is often accompanied by the onset of diabetes (Heisel et al., 2004; Chakkera and Mandarino, 2013).
evidence: Statement of established biological function with citations.

claim: Chronic inhibition of calcineurin is often accompanied by the onset of diabetes.
source: Ca2+ oscillations are responsible for driving the pulsatile secretion of insulin (Hellman et al., 1992; Tengholm and Gylfe, 2008), and the chronic inhibition of calcineurin, which is a common form of immunosuppressive therapy, is often accompanied by the onset of diabetes (Heisel et al., 2004; Chakkera and Mandarino, 2013).
evidence: Statement of clinical observation with citations.

claim: CaNAR monitors the net endogenous calcineurin activity at each subcellular location.
source: On the other hand, CaNAR was able to detect clear subcellular variations in calcineurin activity, which stems from the fact that CaNAR monitors the net endogenous calcineurin activity at each location.
evidence: Explanation of how CaNAR functions based on its design and observed behavior.

claim: The enzymatic nature of CaNAR makes it more sensitive for detecting weak calcineurin signals.
source: The enzymatic nature of CaNAR, wherein calcineurin dephosphorylates many probe molecules, also makes it more sensitive for detecting weak calcineurin signals.
evidence: Explanation of CaNAR sensitivity based on its enzymatic amplification mechanism.

claim: Mice specifically lacking calcineurin in β-cells show impaired insulin production and decreased expression of several critical genes regulated by NFAT.
source: For example, mice specifically lacking calcineurin in β-cells show impaired insulin production and decreased expression of several critical genes, all of which are regulated by the calcineurin-dependent transcription factor NFAT (Heit et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement of previous findings with citation.

claim: Efficient activation and nuclear translocation of NFAT in response to Ca2+ oscillations requires periods of sustained calcineurin activity.
source: The efficient activation and nuclear translocation of NFAT in response to Ca2+ oscillations requires periods of sustained calcineurin activity to produce a cytoplasmic pool of dephosphorylated NFAT that is available for nuclear import (Tomida et al., 2003).
evidence: Statement of mechanism with citation to previous work.

claim: The scaffolding protein AKAP79/150 recruits calcineurin into a signaling complex located at the C-terminus of the L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channel in hippocampal neurons.
source: The scaffolding protein AKAP79/150 has specifically been shown to recruit calcineurin into a signaling complex located at the C-terminus of the L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channel (VGCC) in hippocampal neurons (Oliveria et al., 2007), and the presence of anchored calcineurin within this complex was required for proper NFAT-dependent nuclear signaling in these cells (Oliveria et al., 2007; Li et al., 2012a).
evidence: Statement of previous findings with citations.

claim: Both Ca2+ influx through the L-type VGCC and AKAP anchoring of calcineurin are important for insulin secretion.
source: Both Ca2+ influx through the L-type VGCC and AKAP anchoring of calcineurin are also important for insulin secretion (Bokvist et al., 1995; Wiser et al., 1999; Barg et al., 2001; Lester et al., 2001; Hinke et al., 2012), therefore it is possible that an AKAP-calcineurin-VGCC complex is similarly involved in calcineurin/NFAT signaling in β-cells.
evidence: Statement of previous findings with citations and speculation about β-cells.

claim: Oscillatory calcineurin activity near the ER and mitochondria suggests weak and intermittent NFAT activation.
source: In contrast to the cytosol and plasma membrane, however, the oscillatory calcineurin activity we observed near the ER and mitochondria in MIN6 cells suggests weak and intermittent NFAT activation (Tomida et al., 2003).
evidence: Inference drawn from observed oscillatory patterns with citation to previous work on NFAT activation kinetics.

claim: Calcineurin dephosphorylates the Ca2+-dependent chaperone calnexin and interacts with the ER kinase PERK to modulate protein folding and ER stress.
source: For instance, calcineurin was recently shown to dephosphorylate the Ca2+-dependent chaperone calnexin and interact with the ER kinase PERK to modulate protein folding and ER stress (Bollo et al., 2010), while calcineurin and PERK also jointly regulate insulin secretion (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement of previous findings with citations.

claim: Calcineurin dephosphorylates and activates the mitochondrial fission protein Drp1.
source: Similarly, calcineurin dephosphorylates and activates the mitochondrial fission protein Drp1 (Cribbs and Strack, 2007; Cereghetti et al., 2008, 2010; Slupe et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement of previous findings with citations.

claim: Drp1-mediated mitochondrial division involves direct contact between the outer mitochondrial membrane and ER tubules.
source: Interestingly, Drp1-mediated mitochondrial division involves direct contact between the outer mitochondrial membrane and ER tubules (Friedman et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement of previous findings with citation.

claim: PKA opposes calcineurin activity towards Drp1.
source: Further analyses revealed that PKA, which opposes calcineurin activity towards Drp1 (Cribbs and Strack, 2007), antagonizes calcineurin at the ER and helps give rise to calcineurin activity oscillations.
evidence: Statement of previous findings with citation.

claim: DAKAP1 (AKAP121) binds calcineurin and targets to both the mitochondrial and ER membranes.
source: AKAPs may be involved in locally promoting the PKA-mediated antagonism of calcineurin signaling, and DAKAP1 (AKAP121), which binds calcineurin (Abrenica et al., 2009), in fact targets to both the mitochondrial and ER membranes (Ma and Taylor, 2008).
evidence: Statement of previous findings with citations.

claim: AKAP79 anchors PKA and calcineurin to the plasma membrane in β-cells.
source: AKAP79 is also known to anchor PKA and calcineurin to the plasma membrane in β-cells (Lester et al., 2001), yet calcineurin responses nevertheless appear integrative in this region.
evidence: Statement of previous findings with citation.

claim: Excess calcineurin activity can lead to β-cell dysfunction and death, often involving ER stress and apoptosis.
source: Since excess calcineurin activity can lead to β-cell dysfunction and death (Bernal-Mizrachi et al., 2010), often involving ER stress and apoptosis, this combination of PKA activity and limited access to CaM may help constrain local calcineurin signals within physiologically permissible limits.
evidence: Statement of previous findings with citation and speculation about regulatory mechanism.

claim: CaM acts as both a dedicated regulatory subunit and a promiscuous binding partner depending on the specific target.
source: CaM acts as both a dedicated regulatory subunit and a promiscuous binding partner depending on the specific target (Saucerman and Bers, 2012), and whereas promiscuous CaM is free to associate with and dissociate from target proteins as a function of Ca2+, dedicated CaM remains bound irrespective of changes in the Ca2+ concentration.
evidence: Statement of established CaM behavior with citation.

claim: Ca2+ oscillations in β-cells are often driven by VGCCs in the plasma membrane.
source: In β-cells, Ca2+ oscillations are often driven by VGCCs in the plasma membrane (Ashcroft and Rorsman, 1989; Hellman et al., 1992; Bokvist et al., 1995; Mears, 2004; Tengholm and Gylfe, 2008), and CaM has been found to be locally enriched near these channels (Mori, 2004), ready to be activated by local Ca2+.
evidence: Statement of established mechanism with citations.

claim: CaM is locally enriched near VGCCs in β-cells.
source: In β-cells, Ca2+ oscillations are often driven by VGCCs in the plasma membrane (Ashcroft and Rorsman, 1989; Hellman et al., 1992; Bokvist et al., 1995; Mears, 2004; Tengholm and Gylfe, 2008), and CaM has been found to be locally enriched near these channels (Mori, 2004), ready to be activated by local Ca2+.
evidence: Statement of previous findings with citation.

claim: AKAP79 binds CaM.
source: AKAP79 has also been shown to bind CaM (Gold et al., 2011), thereby serving as another potential source for local Ca2+/CaM and also perhaps lowering the ability of anchored PKA to antagonize local calcineurin activity.
evidence: Statement of previous findings with citation and speculation about functional consequences.

claim: In neurons and cardiomyocytes, calcineurin behaves as an integrator or peak number counter in response to Ca2+ oscillations.
source: In neurons and cardiomyocytes, calcineurin is implicated to behave as an integrator or peak number counter in response to Ca2+ oscillations (Saucerman and Bers, 2008; Song et al., 2008; Li et al., 2012b; Fujii et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement of previous findings with citations.

claim: Rapid Ca2+ transients (> 1 s−1) combined with slow dissociation of calcineurin and Ca2+/CaM facilitate persistent calcineurin activation in neurons and cardiomyocytes.
source: In these cells, rapid (i.e., > 1 s−1) Ca2+ transients, combined with the slow dissociation of calcineurin and Ca2+/CaM, facilitate persistent calcineurin activation (Song et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement of mechanism with citation.

claim: Ca2+ oscillations in β-cells are slow (< 1 min−1).
source: In β-cells, on the other hand, Ca2+ oscillations are slow (i.e., < 1 min−1) (Hellman et al., 1992; Tengholm and Gylfe, 2008), and our results indicate that Ca2+/CaM fully dissociates from calcineurin in between each Ca2+ peak, suggesting that frequency modulation may not be a prominent feature in β-cell calcineurin signaling.
evidence: Statement of established characteristic with citations and inference from experimental results.

claim: Ca2+/CaM fully dissociates from calcineurin in between each Ca2+ peak in β-cells.
source: In β-cells, on the other hand, Ca2+ oscillations are slow (i.e., < 1 min−1) (Hellman et al., 1992; Tengholm and Gylfe, 2008), and our results indicate that Ca2+/CaM fully dissociates from calcineurin in between each Ca2+ peak, suggesting that frequency modulation may not be a prominent feature in β-cell calcineurin signaling.
evidence: Inference drawn from CaNARi experimental results.

claim: Frequency decoding in neurons and cardiomyocytes is based on the intrinsic kinetics of CaM-target interactions where CaM plays a passive role.
source: Furthermore, the frequency decoding observed in neurons and cardiomyocytes is based entirely on the intrinsic kinetics of CaM-target interactions where CaM plays a passive role.
evidence: Statement contrasting the mechanism in neurons/cardiomyocytes with the findings in β-cells.

claim: Cells utilize CaM to actively encode spatial information, which is decoded by calcineurin to ensure oscillatory Ca2+ signals are transduced properly within specific local contexts.
source: Conversely, our analyses highlight a novel mechanism whereby cells utilize CaM to actively encode spatial information, which is then decoded by calcineurin to ensure that oscillatory Ca2+ signals are transduced properly within specific local contexts.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing CaM distribution determines calcineurin activity patterns.

claim: CaNAR2 was constructed by sandwiching the substrate domain of CaNAR1 (amino acids 1–297 from the N-terminus of NFAT1) between Cerulean3 and YPet.
source: Each CaNAR variant was generated by sandwiching the substrate domain of CaNAR1, which corresponds to amino acids 1–297 from the N-terminus of NFAT1 (Newman and Zhang, 2008), between different cyan (CFP) and yellow fluorescent protein (YFP) variants.
evidence: Description of the construction method in Materials and methods.

claim: Plasma membrane-targeted CaNAR2 was generated by in-frame fusion with the N-terminal 11 amino acids from Lyn kinase.
source: Plasma membrane-, outer mitochondrial membrane-, and ER-targeted CaNAR2 constructs were generated by in-frame fusion of full-length CaNAR2 with the N-terminal 11 amino acids from Lyn kinase, the N-terminal 30 amino acids from DAKAP1, and the N-terminal 27 amino acids from CYP450, respectively.
evidence: Description of the construction method in Materials and methods.

claim: Mitochondrial-targeted CaNAR2 was generated by in-frame fusion with the N-terminal 30 amino acids from DAKAP1.
source: Plasma membrane-, outer mitochondrial membrane-, and ER-targeted CaNAR2 constructs were generated by in-frame fusion of full-length CaNAR2 with the N-terminal 11 amino acids from Lyn kinase, the N-terminal 30 amino acids from DAKAP1, and the N-terminal 27 amino acids from CYP450, respectively.
evidence: Description of the construction method in Materials and methods.

claim: ER-targeted CaNAR2 was generated by in-frame fusion with the N-terminal 27 amino acids from CYP450.
source: Plasma membrane-, outer mitochondrial membrane-, and ER-targeted CaNAR2 constructs were generated by in-frame fusion of full-length CaNAR2 with the N-terminal 11 amino acids from Lyn kinase, the N-terminal 30 amino acids from DAKAP1, and the N-terminal 27 amino acids from CYP450, respectively.
evidence: Description of the construction method in Materials and methods.

claim: Cytosolic CaNAR2 was generated by in-frame fusion of a C-terminal nuclear export signal (NES).
source: Similarly, cytosolic CaNAR2 was generated by in-frame fusion of a C-terminal NES (LPPLERLTL) immediately prior to the stop codon.
evidence: Description of the construction method in Materials and methods.

claim: CaNARi was constructed by sandwiching the full-length α isoform of CNA between Cerulean and Venus.
source: CaNARi was generated in pCDNA3.1(+) (Invitrogen). The full-length α isoform of CNA was PCR amplified from pETCNα (Mondragon et al., 1997), a gift of Fan Pan (Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD), using primers incorporating a 5′ BamHI site and 3′ XhoI site.
evidence: Description of the construction method in Materials and methods.

claim: BSCaM-2 binds Ca2+/CaM with a Kd of 2 nM.
source: This reporter features a modified version of the Ca2+/CaM-binding sequence from avian smooth muscle myosin light chain kinase that binds Ca2+/CaM with a Kd of 2 nM.
evidence: Description of the biosensor properties.

claim: Calcineurin binds Ca2+/CaM with sub-nanomolar affinity.
source: Calcineurin has been shown to bind Ca2+/CaM with sub-nanomolar affinity (Hubbard and Klee, 1987; Quintana et al., 2005), therefore we reasoned that BSCaM-2 should offer a fair approximation of how much Ca2+/CaM is locally accessible by calcineurin.
evidence: Statement of established property with citations.
